lead: This unit introduces the basic ideas behind machine learning. After reading, you can describe what ML does, name its main types, and outline a simple learning pipeline.
about: The unit covers seven chapters. Chapter 1.1 defines machine learning and shows everyday uses. Chapter 1.2 explains the three learning paradigms. Chapter 1.3 walks through designing a learning system and what makes a problem well‑posed. Chapter 1.4 lists common challenges such as overfitting and ethics. Chapter 1.5 reviews the essential linear‑algebra and probability tools. Chapter 1.6 studies concept learning with Find‑S, version spaces and candidate elimination. Chapter 1.7 discusses inductive bias and how it affects generalisation. Each chapter builds on the previous one, preparing you for later units on regression, classification and deeper models.

chapters.idea: Machine learning is a data‑driven way to build programs that improve with experience.
chapters.depth: Give the formal definition of ML as a function that maps data to predictions. List applications such as spam filtering, UPI fraud detection, cricket score prediction and traffic estimation. Mention that some syllabi call this "Introduction to Machine Learning".

figure.aria: Data flow from raw data through model to prediction.

chapters.example: A bank wants to label a transaction of ₹5,000 as fraudulent (Yes) or legitimate (No). Features are amount, time of day, and merchant category. Using a simple ML model trained on past 1,000 transactions, the model predicts "Yes" for this transaction.
chapters.trap: Confusing a hard‑coded rule with a learned model; a rule does not adapt to new patterns.
chapters.leave: Detailed algorithmic steps are covered in later chapters.

chapters.idea: Machine learning has three main paradigms: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.
chapters.depth: Define supervised learning with labeled examples, unsupervised learning with only inputs, and reinforcement learning with agents that receive rewards. Note that some syllabi refer to them as "Learning Paradigms" or "Types of Machine Learning".

figure.aria: Tree showing the three major learning paradigms.

chapters.example: Supervised: Classify 200 emails (100 spam, 100 ham) using word frequencies. Unsupervised: Cluster 150 customers by monthly spend and number of rides. Reinforcement: Train a bot to choose the cheapest train seat; each successful booking gives +1 reward.
chapters.trap: Assuming reinforcement learning does not need any labeled data; it still needs a reward signal.
chapters.leave: Algorithmic details for each paradigm appear in later units.

chapters.idea: A learning system is built by following a well‑posed pipeline.
chapters.depth: Explain the five components: task definition, performance measure, data set, hypothesis space, and learning algorithm. State the criteria for a well‑posed problem (finite, computable, and evaluable). Some syllabi call this "Designing a Learning System" or "Well‑Posed Learning Problems".

figure.aria: Block diagram of the steps from task definition to evaluation.

chapters.example: Design a system to predict train delay. Task: predict delay >5 min. Performance: 95 % accuracy on a held‑out set. Data: past 30 days of schedule, weather, and crowd. Hypothesis: linear model y = w·x + b. Algorithm: ordinary least squares.
chapters.trap: Ignoring the performance measure and judging only by training error.
chapters.leave: Specific algorithms (e.g., decision trees) are covered in later units.

chapters.idea: Machine learning faces practical challenges that affect model success.
chapters.depth: Discuss overfitting, underfitting, bias‑variance trade‑off, noisy data, concept drift, interpretability, and ethical concerns such as privacy. Some syllabi list these under "Challenges in Machine Learning".

figure.aria: Venn diagram showing overlapping categories of ML challenges.

chapters.example: A model fits 0 % error on 100 training points but makes 30 % error on 40 test points. Compute the overfitting ratio = test error ÷ training error = 30 % ÷ 0 % → undefined, indicating severe overfit.
chapters.trap: Treating high training accuracy as proof of a good model without testing.
chapters.leave: Mathematical tools to detect these issues are in Chapter 5.

chapters.idea: Linear algebra and probability provide the language for most learning algorithms.
chapters.depth: Cover vectors, matrices, dot product, matrix‑vector multiplication, eigen concepts (lightly). Review probability basics: sample space, events, discrete and continuous distributions, expectation, variance. Some syllabi label this "Mathematical Foundations".

figure.title: Linear model computation
figure.aria: Array showing the values used to compute y = w·x + b.

chapters.trap: Multiplying vectors of mismatched dimensions; here both have length 2.
chapters.leave: Application of these tools to specific algorithms appears later.

chapters.idea: Concept learning uses simple hypothesis spaces and algorithms like Find‑S and Candidate Elimination.
chapters.depth: Define the hypothesis space of conjunctions of attribute values. Explain Find‑S step‑by‑step, version‑space boundaries S and G, and the Candidate Elimination update rules. Some syllabi refer to this as "Concept Learning Task".

figure.aria: Tree showing the most specific (S) and most general (G) hypotheses in a version space.

chapters.example:
Attributes: Weather ∈ {Sunny,Rainy}, Temp ∈ {Hot,Cold}. Training examples:
1) Sunny, Hot → Yes
2) Sunny, Cold → Yes
3) Rainy, Hot → No
Find‑S starts with ⟨?, ?⟩ and ends with ⟨Sunny, ?⟩. G remains ⟨?, ?⟩ because the negative example does not eliminate any general hypothesis.
chapters.trap: Updating G incorrectly by removing hypotheses that are still consistent with all negative examples.
chapters.leave: Discussion of bias and generalisation follows in Chapter 7.

chapters.idea: Inductive bias is the set of assumptions that enable a learner to generalise beyond observed data.
chapters.depth: Define inductive bias and give examples: preference for simpler models (Occam’s razor), linear separators, smoothness. Relate bias to VC dimension and the generalisation error bound ≤ √((h log (2n/h) + log (1/δ))/n). Some syllabi list this as "Inductive Bias".

figure.aria: Plot showing training error decreasing with complexity while test error follows a U‑shaped curve.

chapters.example: Two models on the same data: Model A (linear) has training error 8 % and test error 12 %. Model B (degree‑5 polynomial) has training error 0 % but test error 30 %. Using the bound with n=200, h=2 for Model A and h=6 for Model B, Model A has the lower bound on generalisation error.
chapters.trap: Assuming a more complex model always yields better performance without checking test error.
chapters.leave: Application of bias concepts to deep learning is covered in Unit 5.
